newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Anti-Taleban forces bomb Kabul as lull ends.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban forces bomb Kabul as lull ends.

text.p: Forces loyal to the ousted Afghan government bombed Kabul and launched a blistering assault on Taleban troops north of the capital on Thursday, breaking a two-day lull in Afghanistan's latest war.
The assault, on both the De Sabz pass about 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul, and another pass, Khair Khana, also north of Kabul, began at around 6 a.m. (0130 GMT) on Thursday.

It was followed shortly by a bombing apparently aimed at the capital's main airport in northeastern Kabul, which killed three children and wounded seven people. Witnesses said the airport, used for both military and civilian traffic, appeared undamaged.
The deaths were believed to be the first civilian fatalities in the battle for Kabul since the purist Islamic Taleban militia overtook the capital in late September.
Fierce heavy artillery and rocket duels churned up columns of dust around the strategic De Sabz pass,

"The objective is to advance as far forward as possible," Mehrabuddin Masstan, a spokesman for the commander of former government forces, Ahmad Shah Masood, told reporters at the force's headquaters in Jabal os-Siraj further north.

Masstan said he could not confirm whether any ground had been secured by the anti-Taleban alliance, made up of Masood's troops and heavy weapons and those of the northern Uzbek leader, General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
But he said the assault was "progressing well".
About an hour after the ground attack, warplanes believed to belong to Dostum dropped five bombs over Kabul.
One of the bombs hit a mountainside next to the airport, while two more hit a field about 400 metres (yards) from the airport, one of which failed to explode.

Two other 250-kg (550-lb) bombs landed in the Deh Kepak district in northwest Kabul around 8 a.m. (0330 GMT), killing three children and wounding seven people, witnesses said. There were no reports of injuries from the other bombs.

The Taleban militia fired one ground-to-air missile but it did not appear to hit any of the planes. The assault on the passes is the third in nine days. The previous two attacks were stalemated around both passes, viewed by the former government as "the gates to Kabul".
A senior source in Masood's camp said retaking Kabul from the Taleban militia was both politically and militarily vital.
"We must take Kabul as this will be a sign that we are serious and other provinces will follow (and revolt against the Taleban)," the source said.
A deep, baleful roar announced a clutch of rockets streaming from a large, Soviet-type "Uragan", or "Hurricane", multi-barrelled launcher from the anti-Taleban side.
Orange flashes, white smoke and deafening crashes announced return fire from the Taleban as their rockets landed on the former government's mountainside positions below the pass.
Taleban shells also landed near the old road into Kabul, below the Khair Khana pass.
A commander on the old road reported fighting around the village of Hussein Kot, about 20 km (12 miles) north of Kabul.

The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) agency reported later on Thursday that a commander loyal to the ousted Afghan government on Wednesday launched an attack on the Taleban in Dara-i-Noor, about 45 km (28 miles) northeast of the eastern city of Jalalabad.
Sources close to commander Hazrat Ali told AIP his forces had seized the area after killing many Taleban fighters and capturing at least 20.

Maulvi Saddar Azam, the Taleban's deputy governor of Nangarhar province, of which Jalalabad is the capital, said the attack had been repulsed. He told AIP that at least 250 fresh Taleban fighters had been sent to the area.
No independent account of the clash was immediately available.
